When should the audience be made aware of when AI is part of the creative process? Why and why not? Alexandru, I know Firefly does some embedded details to mark AI-generated images, but I'm not sure how that translates to a final product.
Alexandru Costin
VP of Generative AI and Sensei, Adobe
Yeah. For a long time, as we were pioneering those generative work, we were receiving this media attention and industry feedback that we need to invest in content authenticity. We need to basically help content consumers understand whether a piece of content was digitally edited and, in this case, more recently, fully generated synthetically.
Four years ago, our Legal Department and Dana Row pioneered the creation of the Content Authenticity Initiative, which is a consortium that has 1,000 members now, starting from camera manufacturers like Qualcomm and others, and ending up with websites and content consumption places. Across the stack, we're encouraging the implementation of a digital nutrition label, which we call content credentials, that is a piece of information that describes what modifications were brought to that content, and that's embedded cryptographically in the content itself.
That means that somebody consuming a piece of content with content credentials embedded should be able to read the nutrition label. They should be able to understand, is this piece of content real or is it generated or edited so it does not represent the original intent? This is extremely important in this age where it is so easy to create this content. Imagine the implications of deepfakes in politics.
I mean, this is a really serious issue. This is why we are encouraging a lot of our partners we have. We are working with generative companies like Stability AI, Spawning AI, and others to standardize on these content credentials initiatives, content authenticity initiatives, so consumers of content have the option to first verify, and then trust, a piece of content. Today, you see a photo. It looks real. You implicitly believe it immediately.
In reality, in this new future where all content will be modified digitally and/or generated fully, we need to enable content to embed this authenticity information so consumers can have the right of understanding, then verifying, and then trusting that piece of information.
Hilary Krane
Chief Legal Officer, Creative Artists Agency
I agree with all of that. I believe that some form of watermarking or otherwise being able to trace the provenance of a piece of art back to the consent of the artists who are included should be a part of this kind of nutrition label. The reason I go for a watermark is because it's not just as you're watching the whole content. As we know, somebody can take a clip of that that may or may not have the nutrition label, put it on a platform, and it can be around the world before the artist even knows it's happened to them. If we can embed something that'll pop, that'll show not OK or OK, that's part of the solution. Are we there yet technologically? I don't think so.
With the smart guys sitting next to me working on it and others, and if we take them at their word, the leaders we heard from this couch this morning, I think that we can do a lot to create these tools that'll make it a much safer environment.
Rachel Metz
AI Reporter, Bloomberg Technology
Thank you both so much for talking to me about this. It was wonderful to have you here. Thank you. Let's give them a round of applause. Thank you so much. You guys can just walk off that way. Thank you. It was so nice to see you in person. Thank you. Now I'd like to welcome to the stage Emad Mostaq, CEO and Founder of Stability AI. Emad, thank you so much for joining me. We've got a lot to talk about.
Emad Mostaq
CEO and Founder, Stability AI
Yes.
Rachel Metz
AI Reporter, Bloomberg Technology
Has it been exactly 10 months since Stability AI released Stable Diffusion publicly?
Emad Mostaq
CEO and Founder, Stability AI
Yeah, we released it with Confucius on the Runway 10 months ago. It doesn't feel like it. It feels like 10 years.
Rachel Metz
AI Reporter, Bloomberg Technology
OK. What has changed since then? Because a lot has changed.
Emad Mostaq
CEO and Founder, Stability AI
I think that when we kind of released it, it was building on the research of many others and kind of this whole ecosystem. It was the first large-scale usable model on someone's laptop. That's why you saw such a massive take-up of it. It overtook Bitcoin and Ethereum in three months. It took them 10 years and developer interest on GitHub. Now, cumulatively, the whole ecosystem's overtaking Linux. As you saw ChatGPT and others come, you now have where we are now, which is this technology everywhere and everyone talking about it.
Rachel Metz
AI Reporter, Bloomberg Technology
Let's talk about the new model that's out today. Tell us about SDXL 0.9 and what it means for Stability AI. If we could see some of those images, that would be awesome.
Emad Mostaq
CEO and Founder, Stability AI
Yeah. I think there's continuous evolution. Three of the five Stable Diffusion authors, including the two leads, we're lucky they work at Stability, plus again this whole ecosystem, that took an open model and they just improved it iteratively. SDXL, we kind of scaled it up and introduced some new architectures. It can now do hands.
Rachel Metz
AI Reporter, Bloomberg Technology
Look at that one.
Emad Mostaq
CEO and Founder, Stability AI
That was always a thing because hands are kind of weird. I mean, can an AI do hands? No, can you? It's kind of difficult. Perfect hands, perfect text, photorealistic images now, but also with some mitigations built in because, again, that's why it was important to put it out into the open so everyone could both improve it, and then attack it so it becomes more robust.
Rachel Metz
AI Reporter, Bloomberg Technology
You said mitigations?
Emad Mostaq
CEO and Founder, Stability AI
Yes.
Rachel Metz
AI Reporter, Bloomberg Technology
What does that mean exactly?
Emad Mostaq
CEO and Founder, Stability AI
You have things like we had photorealistic models earlier this year that we didn't release because the time wasn't quite right for it, because you had to build in things like invisible watermarking, working with Adobe on content, authenticity.org, and many others as well, because the technology's inevitable, because you see it emerging everywhere. Part of what we want to do at Stability is introduce standards around that so you can track it, so you can use it, and use it appropriately.
Rachel Metz
AI Reporter, Bloomberg Technology
Right now, if I were to use the latest model, let's say I generated this picture or something similar to it since it's available as of today, would it have some sort of embedded watermarking?
Emad Mostaq
CEO and Founder, Stability AI
Yes. We can't really recall full details about that. There are some official ones, some unofficial ones, because these models become the default that people use. You want to have some way of telling what is generated versus what is not, and that's a huge research area.
Rachel Metz
AI Reporter, Bloomberg Technology
Excuse me. A persistent issue with all kinds of AI image generators, including Stable Diffusion, is bias in the images that are generated. As we know, that stems in large part from the training data. How is Stability AI addressing bias in its Stable Diffusion models? How do you improve this over time?
Emad Mostaq
CEO and Founder, Stability AI
Yeah. I think there was a great research report done by your colleagues, kind of where they looked at the original Stable Diffusion. That was its academic release and the inherent biases because it was taken of a picture of the available internet, and then it reflects the biases of that internet, which is very Caucasian, Western, and others. Part of our mission at Stability is to build a foundation to activate humanity's potential. We are working with multiple governments already on national data sets that reflect the culture of those countries. For example, one of our team members, Makoto Shing, did Japan's Stable Diffusion, where they swapped out the language version because if you typed in salary man to the original Stable Diffusion, it was a very happy man with lots of money.
Rachel Metz
AI Reporter, Bloomberg Technology
Oh, OK.
Emad Mostaq
CEO and Founder, Stability AI
The Japanese version is a very sad person.
Rachel Metz
AI Reporter, Bloomberg Technology
Yes.
Emad Mostaq
CEO and Founder, Stability AI
I think this is the future. Every single country, this is vital infrastructure. They need their own data sets, they need to have their own models, and they need to be able to interact and reflect those contexts and address these biases. We can't do that with black boxes. There's no way to have one model to rule them all that reflects everyone's context.
Rachel Metz
AI Reporter, Bloomberg Technology
You're working right now on different data sets for different countries?
Emad Mostaq
CEO and Founder, Stability AI
Yeah. You take national broadcaster data, you take education data, you take cultural data, and you build from there. I think from a safety perspective, we can't train on the whole internet anymore. The internet's full of garbage. That's one of the reasons we offer opt-outs of data sets, and we have massive investments in refining data sets because we should move to having that as a common infrastructure, both for the proprietary models of the OpenAIs and Anthropics and the others of the world, and also for the open models. You are what you eat, and right now, the models feed buffeted bias garbage. No wonder they turn out a bit weird. Let's feed them better stuff so we have nice free-range organic models.
Rachel Metz
AI Reporter, Bloomberg Technology
If I'm a country and I'm building a data set that I want to be used for a model, who owns that data set then? Is that belonging to the country? Who is in charge of that?
Emad Mostaq
CEO and Founder, Stability AI
I believe it should be national infrastructure. In the UK, we have HDR UK, which organized the national biology and data information infrastructure with federated learning and others. I think this will be infrastructure for every country, so every country has the data sets. We have public broadcasting data that should be used to power AI models.
That will lead to the innovation that we also require to deal with what's coming, because this technology is going everywhere. It's not enterprise-ready. Next year, that kicks off. The only thing that I think that can solve the disruption here is innovation. It becomes vital for countries to stoke that innovation through open data, open models, and innovation enhancement.
Rachel Metz
AI Reporter, Bloomberg Technology
I'm going to ask you a little bit about finance. Last year, Stability raised $101 million at a valuation of $1 billion. We understand you're trying to raise more. Can you talk about how much you're trying to raise?
Emad Mostaq
CEO and Founder, Stability AI
Well, we're not trying to raise more, but we have constant interest. Yesterday, I received eight incoming investor interest notes because we're a bit different. Our total addressable market is all the private data in the world and turning it intelligent, whereas everyone else is looking at proprietary models, which I believe is a race to zero.
Through amazing partnerships like with AWS and more to be announced, our models will be available anywhere because our aim is to have the default model of every modality, commercial variants, and national variants. You can have an Indian insurance stable chat. I think you scale when it's ready and when nearly ready, but you don't try to overscale. It is very difficult because to build these models, you need supercomputers. You need all of these things. Once they're built, they can go everywhere, which is amazing operational leverage.
Rachel Metz
AI Reporter, Bloomberg Technology
There was a recent Forbes article that said particularly that you've exaggerated at times about a few different things. Has that made fundraising any more challenging? What about your existing investors? How have they responded to that?
Emad Mostaq
CEO and Founder, Stability AI
The existing investors, we've been having constant dialogue with them. They've been helping through this process. In terms of additional fundraising, again, we're not actively fundraising right now. The interest just continues to go up because ultimately, it says things like AWS partnership. They built us one of the largest supercomputers in the world before funding. We have an amazing partnership. They talk about technology. We've released another amazing image model. We have language models, code models, and more coming.
I think it's an interesting thing because a year ago, we were a pre-seed startup. Now, we're a scale-up. Next year, we might be a multinational. Growing pains are always there. The ultimate thing is you just have to deliver on what you say you're going to do.
Rachel Metz
AI Reporter, Bloomberg Technology
You mentioned language model. I know that a few months ago, you released StableLM. What's happening with that now? That was like a pretty early version when it came out.
Emad Mostaq
CEO and Founder, Stability AI
Yeah. Next week, we're moving to properly open development. We have a blog and a whole series of papers out with that. We had an alpha. Now, we're going to have a beta of it, which is a massive step up from there. Last week, we released kind of Open LLama, which was a replication of kind of Meta's Llama, except for fully open. Now, it's going to be a highly refined version.
I think what you're going to see with language models now, we just had Qualcomm Cristiano coming on, is that you will probably see GPT-3.5 level performance on the edge by next year if I look at current trends. A large part of that is data. With the right data, you can have a 10x performance increase. That's something we saw when we funded Datacomp on the image side.
With a tenth of the data, the app performed OpenAI's CLIP image-to-text model because the data was such high quality. Again, stop feeding the models garbage. Get rid of all the rubbish, and you will have highly efficient architectures.
Rachel Metz
AI Reporter, Bloomberg Technology
I want to go back just for a moment to the Forbes article. This is something you told my colleague Tom McKenzie recently. He asked you about claims in the Forbes article that you have a tendency to exaggerate. You said, I get excited. I'm curious, what guardrails are you putting in place to make sure your storytelling and your narrative match with what's actually happening on the ground?
Emad Mostaq
CEO and Founder, Stability AI
I think it's surrounding yourself with good people. I think it's not a sign. I was thinking a lot about this. I've asked birds in ADHD. I have a very definitive view of the future. I think that shocks people because we can't deal with exponentials. What's coming now with generative AI?
SageMaker has 100,000 SME customers. Every single one will use this technology at the same time as soon as it's enterprise-ready. This is the biggest economic impact and deflationary thing that's going to hit our economy of all time. I say something like that, it sounds like an exaggeration because I'm definitive. It's what I genuinely believe. This is a difficulty I have. I'm doing the best I can. One thing I don't do anymore is I commit to release dates.
Rachel Metz
AI Reporter, Bloomberg Technology
Oh, OK.
Emad Mostaq
CEO and Founder, Stability AI
My team have been bashing me over the head about that. No more release date commitments, just release when it's ready.
Rachel Metz
AI Reporter, Bloomberg Technology
OK. I understand that because sometimes with articles, I just kind of say, yeah, it'll be sometime this week.
Emad Mostaq
CEO and Founder, Stability AI
Yeah, exactly. We nearly had Stable Diffusion ready. It was super fast, but then it just kind of didn't work. We couldn't release it. Yeah. You do the best you can.
Rachel Metz
AI Reporter, Bloomberg Technology
One concern that people have raised in general about generative AI, both text-based and systems that are creating images, is the extent to which startups and large companies alike are looking to bring in people that can work on the ethics side of AI, people who can develop guardrails within companies. What are you doing on this? Do you have any AI emphasis on staff?
Emad Mostaq
CEO and Founder, Stability AI
I think it's interesting. My background is in ethics and Islamic law, which is a very different type of ethics in some ways. I'm a computational theologist. We have a safety team that we're building out. We work with kind of RLHF teams and others because the models are first deep learning trained. Then you use RLHF, reinforcement learning with human feedback, to bring them towards human. We have our TRLX library, which is the most popular one from our Copper AI lab. We've been bringing in ethicists and others from external parties to look at that. No one's quite sure what AI ethics is right now.
Rachel Metz
AI Reporter, Bloomberg Technology
No one's quite sure what.
Emad Mostaq
CEO and Founder, Stability AI
What AI ethics is right now.
Rachel Metz
AI Reporter, Bloomberg Technology
OK.
Emad Mostaq
CEO and Founder, Stability AI
Part of the thing is to expand the conversation. This is also why we support AIandFaith.org and other things, because the conversation does need to be broadened, because it is so complex. It's hitting every part of society. That's one reason why I was the only AI CEO to sign both of the FLI and safety letters. I think this is a discussion we have to have now, and more voices need to be brought in, because right now, it's mostly guys here in Silicon Valley. I don't think that's correct.
Rachel Metz
AI Reporter, Bloomberg Technology
Do you truly feel that AI is at this moment an existential threat?
Emad Mostaq
CEO and Founder, Stability AI
I think it will be like that movie Her, where we're kind of boring, and it'll bug her off. Thanks for all the GPUs. I could be wrong. That's why I think right now, we need to move before the economic impact happens. This is like COVID before Tom Hanks. We haven't had that moment yet. Everyone's talking about it, your mom's talking about it, but it's not real. Next year, it becomes real, and the economic impacts become huge. The existential side from having crap data that we're feeding these models, the whole of YouTube and others. No wonder it turns out weird. Let's feed it better data now, put some proper standards in place, and build AI that is good for us and doesn't work against us.
Rachel Metz
AI Reporter, Bloomberg Technology
It feels almost like you think that that is inevitable. That's an inevitable outcome. Do you feel like that is an inevitable outcome? I guess from my perspective, I'm like, well, if this hasn't happened yet, there are so many different directions that things could go.
Emad Mostaq
CEO and Founder, Stability AI
I think never the same again is an interesting thing.
Rachel Metz
AI Reporter, Bloomberg Technology
Say that again?
Emad Mostaq
CEO and Founder, Stability AI
Never the same again.
Rachel Metz
AI Reporter, Bloomberg Technology
OK.
Emad Mostaq
CEO and Founder, Stability AI
No head teacher in a school can set essays for homework anymore because of GPT-4. It's never the same again. I think we're going to see a lot of those, a regime change over the next period. This technology is inevitable. It's up to us. It's going to be a bigger economic impact than COVID. Is it up or down? Is it productivity enhancement? Is it job losses? We're not sure about that. On the existential side, we know well, my view is that if you have an AI that's more capable than you, the only way to fully control it and align it is to remove its freedom. I don't know how to do that for entities that are more capable than me. What I can do is I can teach it better.
I think the way that you're brought up makes a big difference. We see that in real life. These models are like really talented grads that occasionally go off their meds. We need to fix that. We need to give them better food, better balance. I think it's more likely that we will have a positive future, especially because the bad guys already have the technology. You can just download it on a USB stick. Boom, you've got it.
Rachel Metz
AI Reporter, Bloomberg Technology
What is the most pressing challenge Stability AI is working on right now? I know you guys are involved in lots of different things. Sometimes, it's hard for me from the outside to see what you think is the most important.
Emad Mostaq
CEO and Founder, Stability AI
Well, the most important challenge for us is to be more transparent when there's so much going on and build the human capital. In particular, the key focus that we have right now is getting language models to the edge. The ability to own your own language models can help you protect against other language models. That will become increasingly convincing. I think everyone needs to be able to own their own models given how powerful they are and how they extend our capabilities. Just like in crypto, there was that phrase, not your keys, not your crypto. I think it's going to be, not your models, not your mind, as we move from here.
Rachel Metz
AI Reporter, Bloomberg Technology
Explain that a little bit more.
Emad Mostaq
CEO and Founder, Stability AI
If you are outsourcing a lot of your cognitive capability to models that are black boxes and they have inherent biases, it's going to be more and more influential on you versus if you have control of your own models for your private data, your private knowledge, be it as Rachel, as Bloomberg, as a country. It's a question of who controls this technology that both extends your capability, but then you rely on increasingly. That's why I think there needs to be open, flexible alternatives to that.
Rachel Metz
AI Reporter, Bloomberg Technology
Might I not want to do that at all? Might I not want to be involved with that period?
Emad Mostaq
CEO and Founder, Stability AI
Yeah. At least you should have the choice. Right now, you do not have the choice. If you want the most advanced technology, it is a black box that can be turned off at any time. OpenAI had an amazing image model, DALL-E 2, that they banned all Ukrainian content from for nine months and all Ukrainians from using. It is completely within their prerogative because of political issues. Imagine if that was the only one and you did not have Stable Diffusion. I do not think that would be nice.
Rachel Metz
AI Reporter, Bloomberg Technology
Thank you so much. It was really great to speak with you.
Alexandru Costin
VP of Generative AI and Sensei, Adobe
Pleasure, Rachel.
Rachel Metz
AI Reporter, Bloomberg Technology
OK.
[Company Representative 2] (Bloomberg Technology)
Company Representative 2, Bloomberg Technology
Time for a short break. Please head out for coffee, stretch your legs, and also, if you would, check out the Chrome Enterprise activation out there, which is an immersive experience in web security. There's a game. I failed it. I think you'll probably do better. Try out the game, and then be back here at 10:55AM for our next set of interviews. Thank you. The program will begin in 10 minutes. Please take your seats. The program will begin in five minutes.

content.text:
Spencer Wang
VP of Finance, IR, and Corporate Development, Netflix
Wang, VP of Finance, IR, and Corporate Development. Joining me today are co-CEOs Ted Sorrendos and Greg Peters, and CFO Spencer Newman. Our interviewer this quarter is Jessica Reeve-Ehrlich. As a reminder, we will be making forward-looking statements, and actual results may vary. With that, Jessica, I'm going to turn it over to you for your first question.
Jessica Ehrlich
Senior US Media and Entertainment Analyst, BofA Securities
Thank you. Let's start with Ted and Greg. You've worked together for over 15 years, but this is your Q1 as co-CEOs. Are there any highlights you want to share?
Ted Sarandos
Co-CEO, Netflix
Well, Jessica, as you pointed out, it's been our Q1 together as co-CEOs, but 15 years working together. In those 15 years, you build a lot of respect and trust in each other to help you get through some trying times. Not to let you down about there was no drama, but this was pretty much a business-as-usual quarter for us, having done this together for so long. Greg and I enjoy the same kind of trust, respect, and shorthand that I enjoyed with Reid for so many years.
I know Greg did as well. It's not as eventful as folks might have thought, and it's really been incredibly and wonderfully professionally stimulating to have a co-CEO and to get to tackle big problems together. I think one of the things that we'll look back at Reid's incredible 25 years at Netflix, one of the great accomplishments, is facilitating this very, very smooth transition and succession.
Jessica Ehrlich
Senior US Media and Entertainment Analyst, BofA Securities
Great. You've recently reduced prices in 116 countries. Is this a more local approach similar to what you did in India in 2021, or is the impetus to enable a successful introduction of password-sharing and advertising tiers?
Ted Sarandos
Co-CEO, Netflix
I can take this one if you want. Jessica, this is really about we talked the last few quarters about further refining our pricing strategy and monetization. If you think back to when we did our global launch in 2016, it was pretty much across the board, a bit of a SCIM approach and not particularly sophisticated in terms of our pricing. Think of this as kind of that next step in our evolution of a bit of a better market fit, product market fit, pricing fit, with the aim of growing our penetration in these markets and also better medium and long-term revenue. Better for our members, better for our business.
I want to emphasize this is not a material to our business anytime in the near term, for sure. It's a lot of countries, but it represents less than 5% of our revenue. It's something that, over the long term, hopefully will benefit us. We can point to an example of success is sort of like what we saw in India. Last year, back in 21 December , we dropped prices in India between 20% to 60%. We saw engagement over the past year grow by about 30%, high growth in paid net ads. Also, revenue, FX-neutral revenue growth actually accelerated from 19% in the year prior to 24% last year.
We're not saying every market's going to play out like that, but that's what it would look like in success.
Jessica Ehrlich
Senior US Media and Entertainment Analyst, BofA Securities
Great. Let's move on to password sharing. What have you seen in your Q1 new market launches, churn as well as conversion? Can you give us any specific color on what you've seen in Canada, whether it's in terms of new subs versus add-ons?
Ted Sarandos
Co-CEO, Netflix
Yeah, I'll take that one. This is an important transition for us. We're working hard to make sure that we do it well and as thoughtfully as we can. This last set of country rollouts have gone well. Maybe most importantly, we're directionally consistent with what we saw in Latin America. Just to remind people what that looks like, very much like a price increase, we see an initial cancel reaction, and then we build out of that both in terms of membership and revenue as borrowers sign up for their own Netflix accounts and existing members purchase that extra member facility for folks that they want to share with.
First of all, it was a strong validation to see consistent results in these new countries because they're different market characteristics, different from each other, and also different from the original Latin American rollout countries. To get to a positive outcome, you mentioned Canada. We're now in a positive member and positive revenue position relative to pre-rollout. That's a really strong confirmation that we've got an approach that we can apply in many different countries with different market characteristics, including our largest revenue countries. In fact, we could have launched that solution. We actually considered that option.
We also learned from this last set of launches about some improvements we can do, especially in areas that matter a lot to our members, things like having seamless access to Netflix as they've always been using it on the go or while traveling, as well as making sure that we've got good tools for them to manage access to their accounts and their devices. All in, we felt based on those results, it was better to take a little bit of extra time, incorporate those learnings, and make this transition as smooth as possible as we can for members. We think that approach also best serves the long-term business goals as well.
We're going to launch this new improved version broadly, including in the United States in Q2.
Jessica Ehrlich
Senior US Media and Entertainment Analyst, BofA Securities
As a follow-up, so the cadence, you just said the US is Q2. How about the rest of the world? Can you give us your thoughts on pricing and whether you have a preference for a current borrower to become a subscriber or an add-on?
Ted Sarandos
Co-CEO, Netflix
Yeah. That launch we're doing in Q2 is a very broad launch. It includes the United States, includes many, many other countries. I mean, we reserve the right for some countries where we think there's a different approach. I would say the bulk of our countries, and certainly when you think about it from a revenue perspective, the vast majority will be rolling out in Q2. You mentioned in terms of pricing, we'll look at that on a market-by-market basis, but obviously, we tested different pricing in these last rollouts than what we tested in Latin America. That gives you a sense about how we're thinking about what is optimal pricing, especially in more affluent countries.
I'll leave it at that. Then in terms of preference, what we're trying to do is create a structure that really supports choice.
That gives an opportunity for folks to spin off to borrower accounts where they think that's the right solution for them, or for use cases, which are legitimate use cases where somebody wants to basically buy Netflix for a family member or something like that. We want that extra member to be in place too. We don't really have, I'd say, a strong preference. We're not trying to steer in one perspective other than using pricing to both satisfy those customer choice goals as well as thinking about long-term revenue optimization.
Jessica Ehrlich
Senior US Media and Entertainment Analyst, BofA Securities
One more on password sharing. Are there any incremental costs? It seems like content, distribution, marketing are already in your expenses. Is the incremental margin 100%, or are there plans to reinvest some of this revenue so it doesn't all flow through?
Ted Sarandos
Co-CEO, Netflix
Well, I'll leave it to—go ahead. Take a second.
Jessica Ehrlich
Senior US Media and Entertainment Analyst, BofA Securities
Go for it, Greg.
Ted Sarandos
Co-CEO, Netflix
No, you got it. You got it. You got it.
Greg Peters
Co-CEO, Netflix
I'd say there's really not, other than just kind of just the general kind of allocation of resources, I wouldn't say there's real incremental costs to this. Of course, we always want to reinvest. As you kind of see with our kind of guidance and our objectives generally, Jessica, we're looking to re-accelerate our revenue growth. That's the path that we're on right now. As we do that, we want to kind of balance gradually increasing margins. You see that in our guide where we're looking to tick up margins a bit to the 18 to 20% range full year relative to just under 18% last year, but balance that with that big prize ahead of us.
Reinvesting to more and more great entertainment for our members and drive that flywheel of more entertainment, more value for members, and ultimately more and more members over time, and then build a really, really big and profitable business.
Jessica Ehrlich
Senior US Media and Entertainment Analyst, BofA Securities
Let's move on to advertising. Netflix appears to have a huge advantage in what's called television advertising. I mean, you pretty much have nothing to lose from a legacy perspective and everything to gain on an AVI platform. Given the limited ad load, premium video content, your humongous reach and engagement with some pretty hard-to-reach demographics, as well as the ongoing mass transition from linear to streaming, your position is enviable. Having said that, you seem to be very careful in your advertising rollout. Can you give us your key learnings to date and what the growing pains have been so far?
Ted Sarandos
Co-CEO, Netflix
Yeah. As you state, we're significantly optimistic about the long-term opportunity for the reasons that you mentioned. We've always expected, and we continue to expect, frankly, this to be a gradual build. It follows a very similar process that we've used in so many other areas where we get in, we learn as we go, we iterate. We found that having that approach yields basically great long-term outcomes as we sort of grow and learn. Co-CEO, Netflix
Yeah, I just want to tell you real quick, we're really pleased with the quarter. 2023 is off to a good start. Netflix is the leading streaming service in terms of engagement, revenue, and profits, and streaming is the future of entertainment at home. On engagement, just yesterday, Nielsen released data that in Q1 to 2023, Netflix was the most watched of any broadcaster or streamer in the US by a pretty nice margin. We have plenty of room to grow. Even with that tremendous amount of watching, we're about 10% of total TV time in our most established markets like the US and the UK.
On revenue and profit, we're growing. Not as fast as we believe we can, not as fast as we want to, but we are growing, and we are profitable. We have a clear path to re-accelerate growth in both revenue and profit, and we're executing on it. You'll see a broader rollout of paid sharing in Q2, and we're going to continue to grow that ad business. We also are aiming to continue to grow free cash flow. As we said, this year, we're going to generate about 3.5 billion in free cash and on increased margins. Remember that this account sharing initiative helps us have a larger base of potential paying members that we can continue to serve and grow Netflix long-term.
That's why we've been so focused on execution. The variety and quality of our much-watched movies, our much-watched TV shows, our must-play games, we're going to keep working to improve discovery, to have buzzier and more creative marketing. Because when we deliver for our members, we deliver as a business. We keep doing that by doing it just a bit better and a bit faster than our competition every month, every quarter, and every year. Thanks, Jessica.

content.text:
Spencer Wang
VP of Finance, IR, and Corporate Development, Netflix
Spencer Wang, VP of Finance, IR, and Corporate Development. Joining me today are Executive Chairman Reed Hastings, Co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters, and CFO Spencer Neumann. Our interviewer this quarter is Jessica Reif Ehrlich from Bank of America. As a reminder, we'll be making forward-looking statements, and actual results may vary. With that, Jessica, over to you for your first question.
Jessica Reif Ehrlich
Analyst, Bank of America
Thank you, and thank you so much for having me today. Reed, the big announcement about the management changes. Can you give us some more color on the process and how you came to this decision?
Reed Hastings
Executive Chairman, Netflix
Jessica, it feels like yesterday was our IPO. We were covered in red envelopes. We IPO'd at about $1. Hopefully, some of you have held the stock the full 21 years. When I think of the evolution, the three of us and so many other incredible Netflix employees, to go from DVD service to streaming leader in films, television, and emerging player in games, and now to have over 230 million members, it's just, Jim Collins probably said it best. He called it a good start. We've had a good start. Honestly, we dream of the whole world finding their favorite entertainment on Netflix, and we shorthand that as entertain the world.
The three of us have been working together for 15 years now, trying to figure out how do we get through this issue, that issue, how do we grow, and I couldn't be happier to complete our succession process. It really started about 10 years ago with the board, trying to think through how could this work. They both have such amazing talents and gifts, and to find a platform where they've been able to contribute is fantastic.
About two and a half years ago, we took a partial step. Ted is Co-CEO, Greg is COO. We continued to just make super progress, and frankly, more and more they've been leading the company, and this is acknowledging really in formal terms how we've been operating for at least the last few quarters. It's just a great feeling.
When I think about the stock appreciation over the last decade, I know that they want to beat that record, and I'm all for that. I'll be Executive Chairman, helping them everywhere I can, but it's really theirs to lead and to do that energy, hustle, and intensity that we've been doing. They're very ready. That's what's driving the timing, and I could not be happier. Back over to you.
Jessica Reif Ehrlich
Analyst, Bank of America
Thank you. Subjectively, I'll just add that this may be the smoothest transition we've seen in media for quite a while. Now, for Ted and Greg, what does this mean for Netflix? Does this signal a change in strategy or approach?
Ted Sarandos
Co-CEO, Netflix
Jessica, let me start with, first and foremost, to thank Reed personally and professionally. He has been, and I trust will continue to be, a role model, a mentor, a friend. In 22+ years, Reed has positively changed my life in every way imaginable. He leaves some big shoes for Greg and I to fill. Fortunately, we have four feet to do it with, so that's a good thing.
In so many ways, the way that Reed's been able to see around corners. That's why he's been thinking about the succession for the last decade. He generously opened up more of a co-leadership model over a decade ago for he and I, and, like you said, two and a half years ago, made it a little more formal. In that time, delegating a lot of the day-to-day to Greg and I.
In that time, in those two and a half years we've been working together, we've been working together for 15 years, Greg and I. In the last two and a half years, particularly, we've been able to build a really trusting, respectful, and complementary partnership, in many ways the same way I have with Reed over the years. I really do believe that this kind of shared leadership model is going to help us to move fast and to challenge each other, to challenge the company, to raise to new heights. I'm just incredible at what we're able to do.
To your point, this is the leadership team. It's been pretty stable, and that's why this steady transition feels so steady. The stability of this team has helped us build a great foundation and a culture that can absorb complexity and change. As you saw in this last quarter, can rise to any occasion. Greg, I just want to say I'm thrilled to be in this with you, and Reed, we can't thank you enough.
Greg Peters
Co-CEO, Netflix
Thanks, Ted. It's a real honor to be asked to take on this responsibility and join you as Co-CEO, and frankly, a pleasure to be able to continue working with some of the most amazing leaders that I've ever had the pleasure of working with, and, frankly, in my opinion, the best leadership team that Netflix has ever had.
I'll just echo Ted's comments. It's been a real fun and rewarding experience to work closely with him over the last couple of years, especially, and I'm tremendously proud of the partnership that we've developed in the shorthand, and really how we have been able to take what are sort of a complementary set of skills and perspectives and seeing different angles to different situations.
Basically, at the end of the day, we have always found or are ultimately motivated by the same things, which is that we want to serve our members, and we want to grow our business, and that is an incredible and powerful aligning process to those different perspectives. I'm proud of the work that we've done over 2022 in the latter half, especially to get some more momentum into the business, but I'm even more excited about continuing to push that into 2023 and follow, the model that Reed has always had of continually seeking excellence and always striving to be better. Looking forward to that.
To your specific question, Jessica, there's no big strategy shift or big culture shifts. Ted, Reed, and I have been working and sort of grinding through our individual perspectives on this for a long time. Really, we look forward to taking things forward as we have been for the last little bit and responding to a dynamic industry and doing the changes that we think are appropriate. We don't have a bank of changes that we've been holding for this moment. Mostly it's continuity and move forward.
Jessica Reif Ehrlich
Analyst, Bank of America
Great. This was originally for Reed, but now given the change in leadership structure, maybe for all three of you, for Reed, Ted, and Greg. One of the best quotes recently was from John Malone, who said shareholders should build a monument for Reed Hastings. John and Rupert Murdoch ran the dominant global media companies in prior decades and were one of the few media executives who've been able to see around corners. Ultimately, they both sold the bulk of their assets. Netflix is now one of the most dominant global media companies, if not the dominant. What is your view of the next 5+ years? Do you need to get bigger, stay the course?
Ted Sarandos
Co-CEO, Netflix
The one thing I'd point out is that what's happening now and what's going to be happening over the next couple of years is that the consumer is moving to streaming. The way that they watch content at home, delivered to them on the internet, on demand, free of the linear schedule and all those things, that is a change, a fundamental shift in the business, and you've got to be where the consumer is. That's what we've been focused on since we started streaming, doing original content 10 years ago, but really realizing that we've we've really benefited from being a customer-first company and meeting the customers where they are.
We've also had this blessing of not having to unwind our traditional media business as we built into this one. We've always been focused on the future and where the consumers are going, and I think our ability to continue to stay focused on that because, I know we've been talking about it for a long time, Jessica, but this is really at its infancy. You think about as big as we've become and all these things that are happening, and in the US, we're about 8% of TV time still.
It's an enormous amount of growth ahead, even in markets where we are very well established. That's the key for us, and I think being able to focus on consumers first has really been our biggest benefit. I think it's what led us to those milestones that you just referred to. Greg?
Greg Peters
Co-CEO, Netflix
Yeah, Jessica, I would say I think that that translates into being bigger, and I think that means being bigger in terms of touching more members around the world, delivering them incredible entertainment. We'll see that in terms of being bigger in terms of the amount of engagement that we can drive, the amount of hours that we're satisfying them.
It'd be bigger in terms of the culture impact. You've seen just incredible cultural impact in terms of Wednesday, Stranger Things, the ramifications that these shows have in terms of the popular culture are significant, and that's going to get bigger too. It also means bigger in terms of revenue and profit streams. We're looking forward to those as well.
Jessica Reif Ehrlich
Analyst, Bank of America
Right. Losing subs in 2022 and the market reaction or valuation reset is akin to August 2015 when Bob Iger called out the early decline of pay-TV subs and the impact for Disney's ESPN. It will take a while for Disney to build ESPN+ into a sports streaming giant, and actually, they may never replace the profitability of ESPN at that point in time. Your pivot seems more broad-based by extending genres and going to new areas, whether it's games, fitness, live, et cetera. Do you see any similarities or differences to that momentous inflection point which has certainly shifted Wall Street's view from subs to profits?
Greg Peters
Co-CEO, Netflix
I'll take a shot at that, and then Ted, maybe weigh in. I think it's a fundamentally different situation. If you look at where we're at, a significant part of what we need to go do is essentially take the core model that we've been operating since we've been starting in streaming, and just execute it better in all dimensions. Whether it's the incredible content that Bella and Scott's teams are producing constantly, how we're talking about that content through the marketing and conversation that we do, the product experiences, and business model innovations that we're doing, a lot of it really fundamentally is about executing that core model better.
There's not a lot of massive pivots away from a traditional legacy business model that we have to go figure out. We're planting some seeds in terms of games and things like that that if we execute well, and we're excited about the progress we're seeing so far, will represent the future potential for us in terms of growth and more profit opportunities. That's exciting. Essentially, a lot of this is just continue to execute the play that we've got, and do it better and better.
Ted Sarandos
Co-CEO, Netflix
I don't know about the similarities, but I would say that this business is really completely about engagement, profit, and revenue. We've got to grow all of those things, and all those things really are tied to executing on the content. When the content's working, the business is working. We grow engagement, we grow revenue, we grow profit. There's an interesting thing starting in July, and you think about from Stranger Things season four, from the phenomena that became and what we've been able to offer up to our members from that day forward.
They went from Stranger Things to Extraordinary Attorney Woo, which was a phenomenal success throughout Asia and in South Korea, but also built a big cult fan base in the US, straight into Sea Beast, which is our biggest animated film ever, straight into Purple Hearts and Gray Man, two of our most-watched films ever on Netflix, and then to August, The Sandman and Never Have I Ever season three, September, Cobra Kai season five, Empress.
Cyberpunk is this animated adaptation of a video game that's been hailed as one of the greatest of all time. Narco-Saints, another monster hit from North Korea, the Jeffrey Dahmer story Monster, straight into Watcher, so back-to-back hits from Ryan Murphy, All Quiet on the Western Front, which just today became the most nominated non-English film in the history of BAFTAs. Only Gandhi has gotten more nominations in the history of the BAFTAs, and that's from Germany with the great Ed Berger, then straight out of there into Enola Holmes 2, a big monster success sequel with Millie Bobby Brown.
You look at all these things that go back and forth, and they go all the way into January now. We'll end the month with You People, Eddie Murphy, and Jonah Hill. Any outlet would kill to have any one of those months as their entire year, and it's our ability to fire on those cylinders and create hits, but more than that, create the expectation that as soon as you're done with this one, there's another one waiting for you.
Jessica Reif Ehrlich
Analyst, Bank of America
Let's move on to something else.
Spencer Neumann
CFO, Netflix
Jessica, may I? Just one thing to add. I know we're going on, but I just think the analogy is kind of fundamentally different. With ESPN and the example you gave, that was a fundamental kind of shift in the industry from 100+ million pay-TV connected homes to cord cutting that's on a path down to mid to high single-digit reductions in that distribution platform each year, and that's moving in that direction.
It's a shrinking core distribution platform where, you see in our earnings letter, the world is shifting from linear to streaming. Even in the largest, there is no country where streaming is more than 40% of share of TV time, and in many big countries, as you saw, it's less than 5%. It's less than 5%, it's less than 10%.
There's an incredible runway still in the shift from linear to streaming. For us, it's about growing into that shift and also obviously competing well, continuously innovating, and improving. What you saw or what we saw and felt when we had that decline in subscribers was really near-term limiters in growing into that big market, but the big market is still growing as opposed to fundamentally long-term limiters in that ESPN shift that you described.
Jessica Reif Ehrlich
Analyst, Bank of America
Right. Let's move on to some of the drivers of growth, both near and medium term, and start with advertising. Your advertising platform's been open only two months, and you've amazingly given some money back to advertisers, indicating in one way that demand is exceeding supply. You guys have consistently said you're going to crawl, walk, and run. How is the crawl stage going relative to your expectations?
Greg Peters
Co-CEO, Netflix
Yeah. Like you say, it's two months. I think the hardest part is actually that first step when you're crawling because you don't really know what exactly to expect as you get it going. Now with two months, it's ridiculously early, but we we've learned a bunch already, I would say. Just ticking through this, I'd say first and foremost is that we were able to launch this very, very quickly, and the tech is all working, the product experience is good, and that's really testament to lots of hard work from both Microsoft and Netflix teams who who worked very hard to make that happen, and it's really rewarding to see.
The other, I'd say, pretty significantly fundamental thing is around engagement, and we see that engagement from ads plans users is comparable to sort of similar users on our non-ads plans. That's really a promising indication. It means we're delivering a solid experience, and it's better than we modeled, and that's a great fundamental starting point for us to work with. Furthermore, now we're seeing take rate and growth on that ads plan is solid.
It's great because partly that take rate and that growth is due to incremental subscribers coming into the service because we have a lower price point. That's $6.99 in the US, EUR 4.99 in Germany, just to give you two examples. That elasticity is a real not only a benefit to sort of growing our ad scale and sustainability, but also to the general business.
I expect to see that continue to actually grow over the year. That take rate fits within the middle of our other plans, which is another really healthy sign. It means that we've got a complementary set of offerings that are working to sort of satisfy different needs for different consumers at the right mix of features and price points. That's quite good.
Another important one, I think, for the investor community, because it came up a lot before we launched, was plan switching. We aren't seeing, as expected, much switching from high-ARM subscription plans like premium into our ads plans. The unit economics remain very good as we modeled. These are all really good initial progress points, but I think it's important to reiterate that, as you mentioned, we're crawling and we'd like to move to the walking phase. We've got a lot to do to get there.
There's a bunch of technical improvements in terms of ad delivery, validation, measurement. We've got progress already on that, more to do in the next quarter or two, targeting improvements, which will be better for consumers, more relevant advertising, better for advertisers in terms of more value delivered, a better set of offerings, products for advertisers to buy. We've got a long list of experience improvements that we know we can deliver that'll deliver more value to both subscribers and advertisers.
There's just also some nuts and bolts stuff that we are learning and improving. Things like how do we do a better job with Microsoft at the ad sales and operations processes. There's so much that we need to do, both companies need to do to better serve advertisers, serve an increasing number of advertisers, and meet that demand.
We're just getting started. We're constantly improving, and we see the trajectory ahead of us. Really, our aspirations are ultimately successively over a period of years to basically build, just like we have essentially in terms of the streaming experience, the best, most effective, highest quality premium connected TV ads experience as a win for consumers and advertisers, and for us as a business.
Spencer Wang
VP of Finance, IR, and Corporate Development, Netflix
Hey, Spencer, Greg. Sorry, Jessica. Spencer, Greg, maybe give a little context on Hulu, what we know about Hulu's advertising. They've had a 10-year head start. How many years will it take us to sort of pass them in all of these key dynamics?
Spencer Neumann
CFO, Netflix
Greg, you want to go first or you want me?
Greg Peters
Co-CEO, Netflix
No, I'll hand it over to you.
Spencer Neumann
CFO, Netflix
All right. Let's see. Hulu, yes, they've had a long head start. They started in the ads business. They have, we would estimate, we obviously don't know exactly, but roughly half of their membership is on the ads tier. It's a multi-billion dollar business for them already, and that's a domestic business, US only, so lower reach, lower engagement than us.
I guess the short story there is we have, given what we've seen and what Greg just outlined in terms of the engagement on our ad plan, the strength of the performance in terms of the monetization, the unit economics, and our ability to scale in a way that is even better than the comparable ad-free plan, plus providing clearly choice that our members or consumers are seeking out because of the sign-up flow that we would expect to be as large or larger over time, certainly in just our US market, and more from there.
I just want to emphasize, it's a multi-year path. We're not going to be larger than Hulu in year one, but hopefully over the next several years, we can be at least as large, and we wouldn't be getting into this business, obviously, as you know, if it couldn't be a meaningful portion of our business. We're we're over $30 billion of revenue, almost $32 billion of revenue in 2022. We wouldn't get into a business like this if we didn't believe it could be bigger than at least 10% of our revenue and hopefully much more over time in that mix as we grow. That's how I see it without putting a specific guide on it.
Jessica Reif Ehrlich
Analyst, Bank of America
You committed to an upfront market spot, taking CBS' prior spot, CBS now [Paramount Plus], which really indicates your long-term advertising goals of being a major advertising platform. Given this is a prime spot on a critical week for advertisers in premium video, it's amazing how quickly you just took that slot away. What's the run stage and what's the timeframe to get there?
Greg Peters
Co-CEO, Netflix
I think, as Spencer talked about it, it will be an iterative process. To your point, it does signal we have big aspirations here, and we think there's a big potential opportunity. We're committed to incrementally execute against that opportunity. Just back to Spencer's point, we are starting from a zero base essentially. Also, we're starting from a history where, as a non-ads platform, we had a lot of folks who basically joined Netflix fully as non-ads subscribers. I think that we'll be working through that over a period of time. Again, our goal and aspiration is that this is a very meaningful and significant source of revenue and profit for us over many years to come.
Jessica Reif Ehrlich
Analyst, Bank of America
When you think about the pool of money that you're targeting linear, let's call it $50 to 60 billion business, seems like the easy money. You've mentioned already, you're just shifting to streaming from linear. We've seen all of the eyeballs move. Now you have basically more scale, more reach, but the digital pool is much larger. In the past, you've said, you've made comments, the company's made comments that you can't compete with Google and Meta, or it would be incredibly difficult to compete with them. Has this changed? Has your view changed?
Greg Peters
Co-CEO, Netflix
Not really. I would say that initially we're competing mostly with that sort of traditional TV advertising pool. Now, I think we can layer into that over time components of what has made digital advertising so effective. If you think about the targeting capability, the fact that we're 100% signed in, fully addressable, if you think about the growing relevance of first-party data and how we do that, those are real big advantages that we can bring relative certainly to the traditional TV world.
Again, the form that we have, at least for the next couple of years will still be in that lean back, primarily in that lean back experience. That lends itself to certain kinds of advertising and certain kinds of advertising goal. A lot of the demand collection component that Google or Facebook is really good at we won't be well suited to compete with that for at least some time to come.
Spencer Neumann
CFO, Netflix
Jessica, just to add to that. The good news, as you saw in the letter, is that that branded video ad market that Greg talked about us focusing on is about $180 billion globally, ex-China and Russia. We got plenty to do and a lot of opportunity ahead of just in that area alone.
Jessica Reif Ehrlich
Analyst, Bank of America
Yeah. No, it's an enormous opportunity, but besides advertising, there's an enormous opportunity in incremental subscribers, as you have mentioned. You have the lowest price service. At least now, you have the lowest price service. Can you frame the opportunity in terms of sub growth? How are you thinking about it?
Greg Peters
Co-CEO, Netflix
Sure. Just to comment on lowest price, again, we don't really think about the pricing question from a competitive perspective. Again, we think of ourselves as a non-substitutable good. When you when you think about Wednesday or you think about Glass Onion, these are titles you can only see on Netflix. That's extremely powerful. Scott and Bella are delivering more incredible titles that are non-substitutable in that regard.
Really, we think about the pricing question as how do we offer a wide range of options for a wide range of consumer needs. We want to make that spectrum even wider as we seek to serve more members around the world and try and deliver appropriate value at those different price points. We're doing a good job of expanding that range.
There are two pools then of incremental subscribers. There's a bunch of people around the world in countries where we're not deeply penetrated, and we have more opportunity to go attract them. A component of that is we've got folks that are watching Netflix who aren't paying us as part of basically borrowing somebody else's credentials. Our goal is over this year to basically work through that situation and convert many of those folks to be paid accounts or to have the account owner pay for them to get a Netflix subscription. Either way we're seeking to sort of monetize the viewing value that we're delivering.
Beyond that, it's back to Spencer's comment. Even our most penetrated market, we're 8% of total TV time, which is potentially a relatively narrow lens to think about the broad competitive entertainment offering. We have huge opportunity to grow the engagement component of that several x we feel like we can get to if we do a great job of executing across all fronts. That represents a tremendous opportunity for more entertainment value delivered. We believe that the revenue flows from that in time.
Jessica Reif Ehrlich
Analyst, Bank of America
Before we get to password turn, just one last advertising question. You now have roughly a decade of producing your own IP. Any thoughts on offering a FAST service over time for your advertising supported television?
Greg Peters
Co-CEO, Netflix
Ted, do you want to take this one?
Ted Sarandos
Co-CEO, Netflix
Yeah. Look, we're open to all these different models that are out there right now, but we've got a lot on our plate this year, both with the paid sharing, with our launch of advertising, and continuing to this slate of content that we're trying to drive to our members. We are keeping an eye on that segment for sure.
Jessica Reif Ehrlich
Analyst, Bank of America
On the password sharing, what will drive consumers to pay $3 or $4 for sharing versus becoming a sub with their own profile? Is it affordability? Is there something else? What do you expect?
Greg Peters
Co-CEO, Netflix
Yeah, I think there's a range of motivations for different borrowers. Some of it is economically driven. Part of what we're trying to do is make sure that we are being responsive to that and finding the right price points, whether in terms of an individual account or an extra member affordance. Obviously, the ad-supported plans give us the opportunity to present a lower consumer-faced pricing in those countries where we have advertising. Part of it's just what we call casual sharing, which is people could pay, but they don't need to, so they're borrowing somebody's account.
Our job is to give them a little bit of a nudge and to create features that make transitioning to their own account easy and simple. We have this basically profile export feature, which allows you to take your viewing history and all the great recommendations with you. To your point, there's a range of motivations and I think a range of solutions that we'll be able to offer to land people in different places.
Jessica Reif Ehrlich
Analyst, Bank of America
Can you provide any details, including the timeframe for converting borrowers to paying accounts?
Greg Peters
Co-CEO, Netflix
Yeah, we've been working hard at this and trying to do some thoughtful experimentation to let our members really speak to us in terms of what set of solutions work for them. That's the testing that you've seen us do over the last couple of quarters. We feel like we have gotten to a good set of features. It's the profile export that I mentioned, but there's also a bunch of account management features that we think are important to making this experience work for folks. We're ready to roll those out later this quarter. We'll stagger that a bit as we work through sets of countries, but we'll really see that happen over the next couple of quarters.
I think it's worth noting that this will not be a universally popular move. There will be current members that are unhappy with this move. We'll see a bit of a cancel reaction to that. We think of this as similar to what we see when we raise prices so we get some increased churn associated with that for a period of time. Generally, what happens is both from the specific changes that we make, we'll see folks come on as new subscribers, essentially borrowers, creating their accounts or incremental monetization through the extra member that'll happen shortly thereafter.
Clearly, our job is to continue to grow value, to have more amazing titles that people cannot wait to see, whether that's satisfying those members who make those transitions or winning back essentially folks who have turned off the service and bringing them back on the service over the months and years to come.
Spencer Neumann
CFO, Netflix
Jessica. Sorry. Because we touched on it a little bit in the letter, but just to reinforce a little bit of what that looks like in terms of timing and guidance. Those dynamics that Greg just walked through, because of that, as we start to roll this out later in Q1, based on the timing, what we talked about is that we'll have modest growth we expect in paid net adds in Q1, but atypical seasonality, where typically Q2 would be a softer paid net ad quarter. It'll probably be a larger paid net ad quarter, and most importantly, what we're most focused on is obviously revenue. That is our primary metric.
What you see is in the guide, these revenue initiatives between paid sharing, rolling out, and then scaling ads, you don't see much of that in Q1, which is why we are we are forecasting 8% growth, FX-neutral, in Q1 revenue. Throughout the course of the year, we would expect to see accelerating revenue growth as we roll out paid sharing broadly across our business, and then obviously scale ads throughout the year, which is a more gradual build. I just want to highlight that, and that is kind of what you are seeing in the guidance.
Jessica Reif Ehrlich
Analyst, Bank of America
Given the revenue drivers of paid sharing and advertising, how are you thinking about price increases in the current year? Is it just too complicated? How are you thinking about it?
Greg Peters
Co-CEO, Netflix
Well, I would say that the two initiatives that you described represent the bulk of our pricing strategy in 2023. We anticipate that they'll both be revenue positive, revenue creative significantly, according to the details that Spencer just offered. Now having said that, our core pricing approach and theory remains the same. We're going to look at the metrics that our members are giving us and telling us, and look for opportunities where we think we've done a good job at creating more value for them.
For a certain customer segment and a certain tier and a certain country, we think we've done a good job at delivering more entertainment for them, then we'll go back and opportunistically ask for them to pay a little bit more so that we can keep this virtuous cycle going, and really invest that back into incredible content and stories. Maybe Ted, I don't know if you want to highlight anything that you see coming on that side.
Ted Sarandos
Co-CEO, Netflix
No, I would just say that it's the must-seeness of the content that will make the paid sharing initiative work, that will make the advertising launch work, that will make continuing to grow revenue work. It's across film, across television. It's the content that people must see, and that it's on Netflix gives us the ability to do that. I'm super proud of the team and their ability to keep delivering on that month in and month out, and quarter in and quarter out, and continuing to grow in all these different market segments that our consumers really care about. That to me is core to all these initiatives working. We've got the wind at our back on that right now.
Jessica Reif Ehrlich
Analyst, Bank of America
You amazingly continue to expand the genres of content, which, as you guys have mentioned, clearly drives engagement. The most recent new genre, which you introduced on your platform at the very end of last month, is fitness.
Greg Peters
Co-CEO, Netflix
That's the time for your New Year's resolution, yes.
Jessica Reif Ehrlich
Analyst, Bank of America
One class online could be the price of a Netflix subscription. While many of the workouts are bite-sized and some are longer, they're simple but deceivingly effective. Can you talk about what your plans are in this area? To the extent you develop more content, it really, as I said, drives value for anyone who would work out anywhere else. How do you define success? Is there anything you can say about partner economics with Nike?
Ted Sarandos
